#756. Christopher Lloyd, 88, Gives Look at Romance With Wife Lisa Lloyd, 56

Christopher Lloyd, 88, shared a sweet tribute to his wife Lisa Lloyd, 56, in honor of the couple's 10th anniversary. The two married in 2016 after meeting in 2005.

If Christopher Lloyd’s calculations are correct, he and wife Lisa Lloyd are celebrating a serious milestone.

The Back to the Future star shared a sweet tribute to the former real estate agent in honor of the couple's 10th wedding anniversary, revealing to his followers that she truly is his density.

“Happy Anniversary @lisaannerocks,” Christopher posted to Instagram Nov. 23 alongside a photo of the two posing together at the Michael J. Fox Foundation's Nov. 14 charity event. “I love YOU.”

The 88-year-old and 56-year-old tied the knot in 2016 after meeting in 2005 when the Taxi alum—who was previously married four times—met her at the Santa Barbara Film Festival.

And the two know exactly how to keep their romance accelerating to 88 miles per hour, as Lisa—who is mom to son Jacob from a previous relationship— has found that having total opposite personalities certainly has its advantages.

“I’ve been with him almost 22 years. My head’s full with a bunch of stupid stuff that you see on the internet,” she shared with People in an interview published Nov. 2. “I watch how contemplative and in control he can be, and I’ve always been more hyper and outgoing than him.”

And those differences are definitely what they’ve come to love even more over the years.

“I appreciate his focus and his calmness,” Lisa said. “Because I’m very outgoing and gregarious. And sometimes he won’t talk. So it’s a balance.”

And Christopher agreed with his wife’s assessment, although he was quick to note that he’s not always as calm, cool and collected as she believes he is.

“Lisa says I’m kind of calm even though I may be going crazy inside,” he quipped. “But I think I’m pretty easy to live with, get along with.”

He also enjoyed that she is always “full of energy and excitement to do this and that.”

“She’s far more naturally social than I am,” the Addams Family actor said. “I’m not a social bug by nature, and it just seems the gel just comes together.”

For a look at more stars who shared the secrets behind their own long-lasting marriages, keep reading.

"I never thought that I would laugh this much in my marriage. That is such a fundamental ingredient of who you are, this insistence on joy," Hermann detailed to his bride of their partnership of over 20 years in Marlo Thomas and Phil Donahue's 2020 book What Makes a Marriage Last. "And I think what sustains our marriage is that I know you love me in spite of who I am, and that is the definition of grace."Seeking out that happiness is key. Even after a particularly robust argument, "One of us will test the waters with a joke—about the very thing we were fighting about," Herman shared of life with the Law & Order: SVU star. "It's like one of us says, 'I'm not saying I was wrong, and I'm not still insisting I was entirely right, but can we at least inch our way back toward the place where we caught at stuff together?' Once that happens, it's a pretty good sign that things are on their way to getting patched up."

They've avoided need for any major renovation by sticking to the same advice they got in premarital counseling ahead of their 2003 vows. Even five kids in, Tuesday date nights are a must and they've held off on purchasing a TV, instead finding other ways to connect. But if Chip were to offer any tip to follow, it'd be to pursue the person you love "like a hornet." Some two decades in, he said, he still feels like the guy hoping to get a second date. "I'm not saying she'd never cheat on me," he explained, "but it's not going to be because I never told her I loved her or because I didn't send her flowers or I forgot our anniversary."

"My first piece of advice is not to take advice from celebrities," Bacon joked of his 36-year union. It's as succinct as their other go-to, "Keep the fights clean and the sex dirty," a phrase developed specifically to end any further chatter about their marriage. Truthfully, though, they make it a point not to let arguments linger, rarely digging in for the sake of the victory. "Honestly, we don't like to fight, so when we actually are in an argument, we're both looking for a solution," The Closer actress explained to Thomas and Donahue. "For the most part we're struggling to get back to everything being okay, because it sucks to fight." Because, when it comes down to it, she continued, "There is no Plan B. No matter what, we want to work it out."

Over 37 years into marriage, the actors have mastered the art of fighting fair. "Tracy and I don't pick scabs," explained the Family Ties alum. "In some marriages, people look at their partner and see vulnerability and they just can't help but go after that vulnerability, like it's a sport or something. We don't do that." That's not to say they don't have arguments. "If I've said something stupid, I have the tendency to want to take it back and make it all okay," he said. "But that doesn't really work." Instead, he follows her lead and tries to give her space. She, in turn, offers up understanding: "Sometimes you just have to say to yourself, 'You know what? He said something schmucky and it made me feel bad. But he's a good person and I'm going to give him the benefit of the doubt that he didn't realize that what he said hurt my feelings.'"

"He still makes me laugh more than any human being," Curtis said about the Waiting for Guffman director on Today in December 2024, ahead of the couple's 40th wedding anniversary, adding jokingly, "and I'm sure there's something about me that he likes. I don't know what it is, but I'm sure there's something."

"I think one of the things that has kept us together all of these years is that we both define relationships as something that's relatively indefinable," the How I Met Your Mother alum said. Through 21 years of career shifts (actor-chef Burtka released his cookbook Life Is a Party in 2019), parenting twins Gideon and Harper and dealing with tough times, "Marriage never stays the same," explained Harris. "When you have sex with the same person over and over, it gets redundant, and so you try different things. Then one day you don't like each other, and suddenly you're not attracted to each other, so you have to figure out how to be reattracted to them—but in a different way because you're aging."Eventually, he continued, you find yourself more attracted to their soul. And then their body again. "It all keeps morphing," he noted. "So in a weird way, we keep falling in love with each other in different ways, over and over."

Appropriately, the comic actors believe their funniness gives them life. And not just in their 19-year union itself. "Whenever we have a good laugh," noted the Can You Ever Forgive Me? actress, "especially a crazy one, when you're like, Oh, my God, and you're almost dizzy—we always assign it a specific amount of time that it added to our lives. And I'm always adding it up. I'll say, 'Okay, that was like two months—I just got two more months to live!'"They put a time limit on disagreements as well. Citing the oft-repeated don't go to bed angry rule, Falcone, said, "I tried it once, and I realized that in the morning I had forgotten what I was mad about. You're not getting any answers if you're parsing out an argument when everybody is tired and possibly had a drink or two. I've never had the thing where you're having an argument at ten o'clock at night, and then you say, 'Well, that was good. I'm glad we got to the bottom of that. We agree. Truce signed.'"

Each having wed before they found their way to the other in 1995, they not only had to navigate a marriage, but life as step-parents to two children apiece. "There is no book that tells you how to do it, so the one thing I figured out right away is that they already have a mom—and it's not me. So what did they need from me?" the Zoey's Extraordinary Playlist actor recalled. "That's when I realized that everybody needs a cheerleader, right? There's never too many of those in your life, so that's what I'll be. I never set their boundaries, disciplined them, or tried to teach them right from wrong. They have parents who do that."The Cheers alum agreed with her stance wholeheartedly. "I think that's really wise, to offer yourself as a friend," he said. "‘I'm not going to discipline you and I'm not going to judge you. What I'm going to do is hang out with you and be there for you.' And that's what you have to do: absolutely, genuinely be there."

The moment same-sex civil unions were legalized in Britain, the music icon and the Canadian ad exec were joined together in a Dec. 21, 2005 ceremony. They repeated the process on the exact same day nine years later once they were able to legally wed. And yet the anniversary they recognize is their unexpected meeting during a 1993 weekend dinner party at the singer's Windsor, England flat, his friend having set the guest list.Every Saturday, no matter where they are in the world, together or apart, the two pen a handwritten note to each other, by the authors' count, some 1,352 letters in all. "There's something very spiritual and real about handwriting," explains Furnish, "and the cards are a chance to reflect on the week that's passed and talk about the week that's coming up." Agreed the five-time Grammy winner, "It's part of the success, I think, of a lasting relationship. Communication is the most important thing."

Having literally Secreted their 40-year marriage into existence ("Six months before I met him, I had these recurring dreams about this person I was going to marry,") they make sure their union has remained front-and-center even as their entire existence has shifted. "Marriage is a priority for both of us. And that means that we act on that and refocus when we've lost sight of the ball," she said. If the surgeon could prescribe one piece of advice, it would be to place that bond above all else. "The bottom line is this: I would do anything for her. Climb any mountain, take any bullet—in the chest, too, by the way. I might do things that justifiably make her really angry at me, but I would never let anything block me from delivering my love to her," he swore. If you appreciate how valuable marriage is to your long-term happiness, he continued, "You will never let anyone touch it."

ABC News reporter Roberts isn't always one for chit-chat. "I don't like the check-in," she explaind. "If you're calling just to say, 'So, what's up?' no, I do not like that." Everyone's favorite TV weatherman, however, is a phone guy. And after years of chafing against his frequent calls, a pal proposed something that changed her stance. "One friend said to me, 'Did you ever think that maybe he just feels comfortable when he hears your voice, because that tells him that all is right in the world?'" she recounted. "And I thought, 'That's very sweet. I'd never thought about it in that way. And if it means something to him, then it should mean something to me.'"Now, she said, "I have learned to take a breath and say, 'Sweetie, I've got some stuff going on, but what's going on with you? Great. I'm glad to hear from you. Got to go. Talk to you later. Love you.' That makes all the difference in the world to him, and it doesn't kill me for two minutes to be nice and sweet." They celebrated their 29th anniversary in September 2024.

The building blocks for their nearly 30-year union began back in their newlywed days, when any fight—one involved the Riverdale actor throwing the talk show host's ring out the window—felt like it could be it. "Early in a marriage, it's easy to let little things become big things—whether it's financial strain or career strain or you have kids and you're sleep-deprived," espoused the LIVE With Kelly and Ryan star. "But Mark taught me to walk away and take a breath. That's when you figure out that it's not a marriage-defining moment."Some hard-earned wisdom, to be sure, but now the parents of three are reaping the benefits. "Anytime you see a couple who seems truly happy, you can bet they've gone through some crazy, crazy stuff together and they've survived," he stated. "That's something to be proud of."

She's an introvert, she said, "maybe a step away from being a straight-up loner"; he's the ultimate extrovert "the mayor of everywhere," as he put it. She's a touch messy; he's "a little OCD" noted the Oscar winner. But, wed since 2003, they've long since learned to let the other do their thing. That's the advice the How to Get Away With Murder lead said she gives to all her soon-to-be-wed friends. "Marriage does not start when you walk down the aisle," she shared. "Your marriage starts when you look over at a person who you love more than anything, and there's something about him—just one character trait that makes you say to yourself, 'Oh man, that's going to drive me crazy. I don't know if I can deal with this.' And then the next minute you say, 'But you know what? I love him.' That's when your marriage starts."

You don't reach the 50-year mark in any relationship by letting disagreements drag on. Any time there's a blowup, noted the Grace and Frankie star, "Usually, I'm the one who apologizes. It's not hard because I love her and can't bear for her to feel lonely for even five minutes." Even better is when she can avoid saying she's sorry to the writer altogether. Her top takeaway, she shared, "Remember, when you're angry at your partner and say something hurtful, you will be more angry at yourself later for having said hurtful things to the person you love. You'll feel angry twice. Not good for your blood pressure, and certainly not good for your relationship."

Few things are more on brand than former New York State Supreme Court judge Jerry declaring their decades-long union works because he usually lets the Judge Judy icon win. But for his bride it's more about knowing you're not always going to like the final verdict. Their 12-year marriage dissolved in 1990 when he couldn't be the caretaker she needed following her father's death. Yet, when they got back together one year later and quickly remarried, she had no delusions that he was suddenly going to be the type to run the household or take the lead on birthday plans. "Every relationship is different, but there is a common thread of unhappiness, and that unhappiness comes from trying to make another person different from who they are. You can try, but they're always going to resent it," she explained matter-of-factly. "I don't think you should marry anyone with the expectation of changing who they are."

The Lost alum would be, well, lost without his longtime love, who he married in 1993. As he explained to E! News in April 2025, "My wife—being patient as I traipse around the world, going from job to job—she's kept our family stable. She's been fantastic."

Calling her a "very patient woman," the actor said his wife and their two sons keeps him "humble no matter what's happening."

"They shape my values," he added. "It's great to have that perspective and North Star."

#754. Stokes registers for 2027 IPL auction

Ben Stokes has entered his name for the 2027 IPL auction; former England captain is among 30 players listed at the maximum base price of INR 2 crore [£165,000]

Former England captain Ben ‌Stokes has registered for the 2027 Indian ‌Premier League auction, Cricinfo reported ​on Tuesday, with the all-rounder among the long list of names potentially set to go under the hammer in ‌Goa on December 16.

IPL rules barred players ​who skipped the mega auction in 2025 from registering for the ​following mini auction, ⁠meaning Stokes could ⁠not return to the auction pool until ‌2027.

Indian media reported, however, that the 35-year-old has been ‌granted permission by the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) to enter this ⁠year's auction.

The 35-year-old has been listed at the maximum base price of INR 2 crore [£165,000] with the players' auction held next month, a day before England's first Test on their tour of South Africa, live on Sky Sports.

England internationals Jonny Bairstow, Sam Billings, Sonny Baker and Tom Curran are also in the 30-player group with the maximum base price.

Stokes, who retired ​from international cricket ​this year, last played ​for Chennai Super Kings in ⁠2023 and has scored 935 runs and taken ⁠28 wickets in ​45 IPL matches across five ​seasons.

#753. Germany news: Plans for Rwanda migrant hub come under fire

Human rights groups have slammed plans by Germany and four other EU states to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda. In other news, business start-ups in Germany are on track to reach the highest level since 2015.

Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow, thank you for staying with us. Tschüss!

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.

Pistorius said ‌criticism of ​Ukraine's deep strikes in ​Russia was ​misplaced.

In particular, Pistorius responded to US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby, who said Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war."

The German defense minister said "criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military and military-used targets" was "quite a ​stupid thing."

"Instead ‌of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on... energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius said.

He added that attacks inside ⁠Russia ​against ​non-civilian targets ​and sites used ‌by the military ​are ⁠legal and legitimate targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Former US President Joe Biden's new autobiography "Promise Me, America" hit bookshelves on Tuesday, and it features anecdotes about several global leaders, including former German Chancellor Angela Merkel.

In the book, Biden dished on conversations that he and Merkel had about his predecessor and later successor, Donald Trump.

Citing conversations from early 2021, Biden wrote, "Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts."

"She also wondered," wrote Biden, "why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel."

Merkel and Trump were often at odds over issues tied to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's dependence on Russian energy but one of the most infamous meetings between two came in the Oval Office in March 2017, when Trump awkwardly refused to shake hands with the German leader during a press availability despite photographers loudly encouraging him to do so.

Merkel reflected on the moment in her own 2024 memoir "Freedom" saying that after initially approaching Trump as someone "completely normal" she quickly sensed that he viewed their public meetings as a kind of "you or me" competition.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a plan by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers ​to a deportation hub ​in ‌Rwanda.

Türk said he had not yet ‌seen the draft proposal ‌but that ​his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by ​the proposed transfer of people from five ⁠European Union ​countries to ​Rwanda, where they have no ​genuine connection and ‌which has its own set ​of ⁠human rights challenges."

Instead, he called ⁠for ​a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights."

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck" (see entry below).

New figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.

Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.

France was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.

The Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.

Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%)  had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.

Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.

Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.

The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.

VC said that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.

"The ball is now in the employer's court," VC said in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.

Lufthansa, meanwhile, said it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 new cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.

VC said it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.

The airline also said arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.

The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.

Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.

The ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.

The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, said the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.

The ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.

Spranger said the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.

A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.

The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck."

Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp said that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.

"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he said.

"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support."

In a statement issued after the announcement of the plans, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.

"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.

"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it said.

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.

"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.

"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals."

The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.

According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

The plan to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion,  German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on Tuesday.

He said that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.

Most of the new funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius said in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.

He said Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously announced, as well as new radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.

He also said that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.

Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.

He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.

"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.

He said Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.

Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and new transport links.

Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.

He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.

In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.

Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.

The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.

The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.

Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that  sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.

The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.

Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents."

It also said that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank."

The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.

The commission said stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.

The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.

Some 286,000 new businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).

The BVR said the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.

However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.

In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.

The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.

The association also said that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.

DW's newsroom on the Rhine in Bonn wishes all readers a guten Tag!

Plans announced by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.

Migration hard-liner Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, one of the main advocates of the plan, has, however, given assurances that it will be executed "in line with human rights" and "in accordance with European and German law."

Meanwhile, more new businesses are expected to open in Germany this year than has been the case since 2015, a rise partly driven by the growing presence of artificial intelligence.

And internal documents leaked by whistleblowers from Deutsche Bank, a lender that has had more than its fair share of scandals in the past, have exposed more cases of malpractice and misconduct in recent years, media say.

#751. Dax Shepard Details Depression Over "Abusive Husband" Allegations

Dax Shepard said he's experiencing depression over allegations that he's an "abusive husband" to wife Kristen Bell after the Frozen star revealed he flirts with her by complimenting other people.

Dax Shepard is getting candid about his mental health amid controversy.

The Armchair Expert host shared he's experiencing depression over allegations that he's an "abusive husband" to his wife of 13 years Kristen Bell.

"I generally don't have depression, but I've had it," Shepard shared on the Nov. 23 episode of his podcast. "I'm so tired and I've been taking so many naps, and I got to say there that is a silver lining."

The 51-year-old went on to describe the "continuing narrative" that he allegedly mistreats his wife as "very offensive," noting how the accusations first started last year when some social media users misconstrued an inside joke the Frozen star had made in an Instagram post celebrating their wedding anniversary.

"We were watching Dateline one time, and everyone kills their rich spouse," Shepard recounted to guest Zosia Mamet, explaining how he was "complimenting Kristen" by telling her at the time, "'You know, I’m heavily incentivized to kill you, but I’m not going to.’"

Though Bell had told him that the quip was "one of the most romantic things anyone said to her," Shepard said a "cottage industry of women" online didn't think so and accused him of being a "dangerous man."

And when Bell recently revealed that her husband unconventionally flirts with her by complimenting other people while in her presence, Shepard said the allegations that he's a "controlling" spouse only snowballed.

"Of course, the controlling husband would try to control the narrative," Shepard sarcastically remarked, before agreeing to Mamet's assessment that he's "f--ked."

In fact, Shepard has emphatically denied claims that he mistreats Bell, with whom he shares two daughters.

"I don't ever yell at my children. I don't swear at them. I don't yell at my wife," he said on Armchair Expert's Nov. 9 episode. "To have given it my all to be the opposite of what, now, some group of people is saying I am is hard."

"I find it deeply insulting to my wife, additionally," Shepard added. "She's sitting in a house with her two daughters and modeling some abusive relationship? It's very offensive to her."

For a real look at Shepard and Bell's home life with their kids, read on.

Dax Shepard shared a kiss with daughters Lincoln and Delta, who were dressed in chic French-style ensembles that included striped tees and berets. Kristen Bell captioned the post in honor of her husband's birthday in January 2025, "I cannot imagine life without you."

Kristen had a rosy time going "flower farming" with her girls during a trip to S.E. Daugherty & Sons Farms in Nashville in July 2025.

Delta and Lincoln took in the sunset view with their furry friend in summer 2025. As Kristen put it in her Instagram post, "Lake life : 5 out of 5 jalapeños."

The Parenthood alum gave a kiss to his daughter while out to dinner.

Kristen provided a glimpse at their family bond while honoring Dax's sobriety anniversary in September 2025.

"This is what 21 years of sobriety looks like," she wrote. "Lots of hugging. Hugging everyone and everything. Hugging life. Thank you for getting sober, @daxshepard. I am eternally grateful to have you. We all are."

The father-daughter duo cuddled during a sweet moment in another snap.

The family got emotional while sharing an embrace at school.

Dax proved he's the ultimate girl dad while sharing a hug with his kiddo, clan in lemon pajamas.

When his daughter got too tired on a boat outing, Dax carried her on his lap as he sat at the wheel.

#749. Blend public cash and private innovation to unlock drug development

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Victor J. Dzau is a professor of medicine at Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA.

Will Ellaissi is head of product at Switchboard, MD, Atlanta, Georgia, USA.

Emily L. Shambaugh is special assistant and policy adviser at Duke University in Washington DC, USA.

A fresh model of research and development is needed to incentivize manufacturers to go after diseases that aren’t sure bets.Credit: Stanislav Gvozd/Getty

For decades, most countries have followed the same model of biomedical innovation. Basic research is undertaken mostly by universities and academia, and private industry leads the translation of research into health solutions1.

This approach has generated extraordinary drugs and therapies as well as economic success. In 2022, the pharmaceutical sector contributed US$2.3 trillion — or around 1.7% — to global gross domestic product (GDP) and supported 75 million jobs2.

How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science

How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science

However, market failures have been common. Companies have underinvested in developing therapeutics for common diseases with poorly understood biological mechanisms, such as depression, anxiety and kidney disease, because they consider them too commercially risky or unprofitable to pursue3.

To address this gap, we propose an adapted innovation model based on mission-driven public–private partnerships (PPPs), in which government acts as a leading strategic investor. By bringing together the best scientists in academia and industry and lowering risks in industry development in areas of public need and for diseases with limited understanding, this model would accelerate translation, advance health and increase economic returns.

Here, we outline how it would work. It will require systems to ensure affordable access to drugs and therapies, as well as revenue sharing between public and private partners to guarantee public benefits and to support investments in innovation.

Complex diseases that affect swathes of the population create persistent health and economic burdens. Yet, the current biomedical innovation model has proved limited in addressing evolving health needs. Because private investment is guided by assessments of risk and return, it tends to favour diseases with well-defined biological mechanisms and high commercial potential. Diseases that are biologically complex, varied or associated with uncertain markets remain underexplored.

For example, in 2023, more than 300 million people globally had depression. The condition will cost the global economy an estimated $12 trillion between 2025 and 20504. In the United States in 2024, one in five people reported that they had received a diagnosis of major depressive disorder during their lifetime, resulting in an economic burden of $334 billion annually across health-care, household-related and workforce costs5. Yet, the leading drug class for depression (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) has remained unchanged since the 1970s6.

The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care

The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care

Other chronic diseases impose similarly large burdens. For example, chronic kidney disease affects around 800 million people worldwide — nearly one in seven — and is projected to become the fifth leading cause of death globally by 2040 if current trends continue7,8. Yet, existing therapies cannot stem its toll on human lives.

Antimicrobial resistance is another example, which is associated with 4.7 million deaths globally each year and could contribute to 10 million deaths annually by 2050. Increased treatment costs for people with resistant infections amount to $1 trillion every year9. The antibiotic development pipeline has been depleted over time as economic factors render companies’ return on investment lower than that for other drug classes9. These factors include insufficient funding for research and challenging business models, given the short duration of antibiotic treatments and the need to reserve successful new antibiotics as drugs of last resort, to be used after all other options have failed.

Bringing a therapy to market from discovery can take 10–15 years and cost anywhere between $880 million and $2.3 billion10,11. The majority (90%) of drug candidates fail after entering clinical studies, clinical trials and drug-approval processes12. And companies won’t invest if they are unsure whether a drug will be profitable.

Consequently, many diseases and conditions have no or few available therapies or only modestly effective options13. What’s needed is a mission-driven strategy to guide scientific capabilities and industry development towards areas of public need by elucidating biological mechanisms and aligning incentives for diseases in which market forces alone are insufficient14.

We propose addressing this misalignment of incentives by reconceptualizing the government’s role in therapeutic advancement through a model of mission-driven PPP. Complementing existing grant-based systems, the model would position the government as a principal investor in select areas of therapeutic development.

The government would thus influence which areas of health and science receive concentrated attention and how successful outcomes are deployed for the public good. Such a model could address specific national needs and global challenges. Here are seven components.

Technicians at work in a pharmaceutical factory.Credit: Getty

Select disease targets. We propose the establishment of a government-appointed independent advisory body or commission tasked with identifying priority disease targets using transparent, evidence-based criteria, including disease burden, economic cost, scientific readiness and demonstrable market failure. Further criteria to gauge and consider public input into the selection process could be implemented to ensure public trust.

Set up collaborations. A national government, acting alone or as part of an international consortium, would assume a leading role in supporting basic research into biological mechanisms. It would do so by bringing together basic scientists from academia and translational experts from industry to reduce risks in translational development. Private industry would contribute expertise in drug development, clinical trials, regulatory strategy, manufacturing and commercialization.

Provide initial investments. The proposed PPP would not replace existing grant-based systems or market-driven innovation; rather, it would act as a complement by targeting disease areas in which market risks and incentives consistently fail to generate sufficient private investment. The approach could yield fresh therapies and reduce the cost of care to society while generating revenue from new products.

Could measuring immune health reshape medical care?

Could measuring immune health reshape medical care?

In the United States, we propose a federal investment of one billion dollars annually over ten years, directed to specific disease areas. That is less than 1.8% of total US government spending on biomedical research, which was $54.5 billion in 2024. This would be supplemented by smaller investments of 10–20% of one billion dollars from a consortium of philanthropic foundations and industry partners joining the initiative in response to a request for application. Given the high costs of bringing a new drug to market, a $10-billion total investment should provide the scale and time needed to pursue about three major disease targets10–12.

Feed revenues back in. Public return is a defining feature of the PPP. Existing biomedical funding structures are mainly grant making, with the implication that public benefit will emerge indirectly through the downstream health improvements and economic growth spurred by discovery. By contrast, this PPP framework would directly incorporate public accountability as well as returns.

The government would need to leverage its status as a majority investor to ensure access, fair pricing and affordability. It might require conditions such as agreements to ensure access. Pricing frameworks could incorporate a value-based approach to pricing, in which health insurers offer reimbursements determined by a drug’s value for patients. Affordability conditions, such as reasonable-pricing clauses, would also serve as powerful leverage.

#748. Parker still winless as Portsmouth beat West Ham

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Portsmouth and West Ham United at Fratton Park on Tuesday night; Odin Bailey scores the only goal as Pompey beat Hammers to leave Scott Parker without a win.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Scott Parker's winless start to life as West Ham boss continued as Odin Bailey netted his first Portsmouth goal in a 1-0 victory at Fratton Park.

Parker has lost two and drawn two since replacing Nuno Espirito Santo in the Hammers dugout, with the east Londoners without victory in six and 11 points off the top of the table.

The Championship's top scorers West Ham failed to scored for the first time this season, despite hitting the woodwork twice, as Bailey's first-half strike was enough for Portsmouth to rise to 10th.

Academy graduate goalkeeper Finlay Herrick was drafted into the Hammers starting XI at the weekend in place of Mads Hermansen, but the 20-year-old had a first half to forget after keeping his spot in the team.

He got away with flapping at Bailey's fourth-minute corner as Ebou Adams scooped the ball over the bar from close range.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

But Herrick was punished for a weak punch at Tyrese Shade's dangerous cross from the right in the 31st minute and his poor connection went straight to Bailey, who thumped his finish under the keeper.

Bailey's first goal since arriving from Stockport was a bad omen for the Hammers, who had failed to win on the previous nine matches they had conceded first this season.

Middlesbrough 2-1 Swansea City: Will Lankshear steers Boro back to the top of the Championship

Burnley 2-2 Blackburn: Todd Cantwell penalty earns draw as Rovers players send message to Tony Mowbray

Lincoln 0-1 Wrexham: George Thomason nets winner for Red Dragons

Stoke 1-0 Birmingham: George Hirst scores as 10-man Potters claim win

There had been a general air of nervousness about the visitors - without a win since October 17 - but they still created strong openings.

Jarrod Bowen showed pace on the right before his shot was pushed on to a post by Nicolas Schmid in the early stages.

Portsmouth goalkeeper Schmid has come under scrutiny of his own and did well to deny Joel Piroe twice but also had his own punching gaffe.

The Austrian managed to punch Arne Engles' corner behind him, but Madiodio Dia spared his blushes on the line as Mohamadou Kante lurked for a tap-in.

The Hammers had a claim for a penalty at the start of the second half when Konstantinos Mavropanos flung himself to the ground under Adams' tackle, but Andrew Kitchen waved the shouts away.

Engels struck a free-kick into Schmid's midriff before the Belgian was set up with a golden headed chance by Edvin Austbo, but his effort flew over the arriving Tomas Soucek and wide.

The hosts still offered a threat and almost doubled their lead in extraordinary style when Abu Kamara volleyed a raking through-ball wide.

It seemed to add a desperation to West Ham's attacking as Austbo headed at Schmid before the keeper produced a showstopping save to push Soucek's rasping shot on to the crossbar, but they could find an equaliser.

#746. Ashe Addresses Rumor Her Song "Stop the Wedding!" Is About Finneas

After Ashe's hit single "Stop The Wedding!" was released, three weeks before Finneas married Claudia Sulewski, she reacted to claims the track was inspired by unrequited feelings for her collaborator.

Ashe wasn't wasting her night out and wearing her heart out over these romance rumors.

Nearly three months after the singer released her track "Stop The Wedding," she addressed speculations that she was inspired by an unrequited love for longtime friend and collaborator Finneas ahead of his August nuptials to Claudia Sulewski.

"We were in a full band. People were very upset about that," Ashe explained on a recent episode of the Big Small Talk podcast. "Some people thought that I wrote 'Stop the Wedding!' to stop his wedding with Claudia, which is the most insane thing, because I had just gotten married."

The 33-year-old (born Ashlyn Rae Willson)—who tied the knot with John Clark Canada in October 2025—noted that the rumors grew more and more ridiculous over time.

"It's so stupid until it's funny," she explained. "You let yourself get mad about it, and then it becomes funny and then you let it go."

Ashe—who co-released The Dream (2025) with Finneas and The Favors—emphasized that if she had actually written the song about Billie Eilish's older brother, it wouldn't have gotten her guy.

She sardonically added, "So, you're going to pick me now, right? Like what?"

Ashe previously revealed that the song was actually inspired by her "horrifying" marriage to her ex-husband—whom she has not publicly identified—after their 2019 split.

"Do I wish I'd had that advice at the time? 1,000 percent," she told the BBC in October. "If someone had given me the insight that I was not stuck, and that I could run, I could have changed things sooner."

"Maybe not at the altar," she acquiesced. "Maybe weeks before—but it was something I really could have used."

As their relationship continued while her career thrived, she felt her forever falling apart. In fact, he was anything but a fan after she decided to pivot from songwriting—including co-writing Demi Lovato's "You Don't Do It for Me Anymore" in 2017—to hitting all the right notes herself.

"I remember him saying, '[After this] no-one's ever going to love you for you,'" she recalled. "'Anyone you meet now is going to meet you as Ashe, and I met you before.'"

"It was truly manipulative, and it kept me stuck," she admitted. "It kept me stuck for a long, long time."

But Ashe eventually found the guy of her dreams in Canada.

As she put it, "I'm in a happy, healthy relationship and I have total autonomy over my own life."

#744. Jodie Sweetin's Daughter Zoie, 18, Is Her Twin in Rare Photo

Jodie Sweetin shared a rare photo posing alongside her and ex Cody Herpin’s lookalike daughter as they enjoyed a girls’ night in Los Angeles: “Had the best time out with Zoie!”

A closer look inside Jodie Sweetin’s bond with her kiddos? You got it, dude.

The Full House alum shared a rare photo of her and ex Cody Herpin’s 18-year-old daughter Zoie enjoying a festive girls’ night out together—and they couldn’t cut it out with their uncanny resemblance if they tried.

“Had the best time out with Zoie!” Jodie captioned a Nov. 23 Instagram post featuring a selfie of the mother-daughter duo. “Nothing better than getting dressed up and spending a fun night together.”

In the photo, Jodie, 44, gave the camera a wide smile as her daughter leaned in close by her side with her tongue sticking out during the pair’s outing at the Westfield Century City mall’s holiday village in Los Angeles.

And while the adorable snap will certainly fill the hearts of Full House fans everywhere, it’ll also have them saying “Oh, Mylanta!” After all, Zoie was practically her mom’s twin as she rocked a soft glam look for the occasion.

And it’s safe to say the teen had just as much fun as the Fuller House star. As she commented under the post, “Love u mama.”

Recently, Jodie—also mom to daughter Beatrix, 16, with ex Morty Coyle—shared insight into Zoie’s future plans.

“She wasn’t quite sure what she wanted to do, and she had an opportunity to play soccer somewhere at community college and get a scholarship, so she was like, ‘Yeah, let me like save some student debt and all of that while I’m figuring out what I want to do,’” Jodie said during her July 15 appearance for The Dory Jackson Interview. “I’m so proud of her because this was absolutely, I think, the right next step for her.”

Sweetin continued, “I just wanted her to feel like she was in control of what comes next. She’s like putting the pieces together. She can’t put the dishes in the dishwasher, but she’s putting the pieces of her life together, so I’ll take the small wins where I can get them.”

As for whether she’s ready to be an empty nester with Beatrix not too far from adulthood?

“I don't think it'll ever be empty,” Jodie—who married husband Mescal Wasilewski in 2022—explained. “Do we ever empty the nest these days? You know, hardly. At some point, my husband and I would like to move out of LA and that will obviously come once they're done with school and all that kind of stuff. I'd still want a place here so they can fight over who gets to stay in mom's condo or something.”

Even so, how rude it would be to assume she’d stifle her daughters’ independence.

“I'm not one of those parents who's been really afraid of their kids growing up,” she said. “If anything, I have enjoyed watching who they have become.”

#743. Lankshear steers Boro back to the top of the Championship

Middlesbrough vs Swansea City. EFL Championship.

Riverside StadiumAttendance: Attendance26,960.

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Middlesbrough and Swansea City at the Riverside Stadium on Tuesday night; Will Lankshear returned to the starting line-up with the winning goal to send Boro back to the top of the table.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Will Lankshear was back among the goals as Middlesbrough cemented their position at the top of the Championship with a 2-1 win over Swansea City.

Lankshear had missed the final two games prior to the international break because of a hamstring injury, and was only afforded a late substitute appearance in Saturday's win over Bristol City.

Having been restored to the starting line-up at the Riverside, the Championship's leading scorer claimed his 14th league goal of the season to reestablish his side's lead in the second half after Joseph Opoku's driven finish had cancelled out Myles Peart-Harris' opener.

Lankshear's winner came nine minutes into the second half, but the England Under-21 international was also heavily involved in the slick passing move that led to Boro opening the scoring in the ninth minute.

Lankshear's first-time pass released Neto Borges into the left of the area and when he squared across the face of the box, Peart-Harris slotted home a first-time strike of his own to claim his first goal since joining Middlesbrough in the summer.

Boro's lead lasted 13 minutes, with Swansea levelling when Lankshear was at fault at the opposite end of the field.

The striker bundled over Elijah Just on the edge of the area to concede a free-kick. Ben Cabango's goalbound header was nodded off the line by Ashley Phillips, but the ball broke to Opoku, who drilled home an excellent low finish from the edge of the area.

Portsmouth 1-0 West Ham United: Scott Parker stays winless as Odin Bailey nets Pompey winner

Burnley 2-2 Blackburn: Todd Cantwell penalty earns draw as Rovers players send message to Tony Mowbray

Bolton 1-1 Portsmouth: Sam Dalby earns point for Trotters

Lincoln 0-1 Wrexham: George Thomason nets winner for Red Dragons

Swansea 2-2 West Brom: Managerless Swans hit back twice for a point

Stoke 1-0 Birmingham: George Hirst scores as 10-man Potters claim win

Boro went close to regaining their lead when Riley McGree fired a first-time strike just wide from a corner, and threatened again just before the interval when Peart-Harris volleyed over at the back post after David Strelec flicked Borges' cross into his path.

Swansea remained a threat though, and six minutes into the second half Adilson Malanda played Eom Ji-sung onside as Opoku's through ball unpicked the Boro defence, only for goalkeeper Radek Vitek to burst from his line to keep out the midfielder's shot with his foot.

It was a crucial save as just three minutes later Boro were scoring their second goal at the other end. Callum Brittain's pass sent Peart-Harris breaking away down the right, and when he squared the ball across the face of goal Lankshear was left with the easy task of tapping home.

Sebastian Berhalter should have added a third goal with 18 minutes remaining, but after coming off the bench the American midfielder dragged a shot wide from the right of the area.

His fellow replacement, Max Arfsten, also wasted a good late opportunity, drilling a low strike straight at goalkeeper Lawrence Vigouroux.

#741. Watford set to appoint former Romania boss Iordanescu

Edward Iordanescu's most recent job was with Legia Warsaw, who he left in October 2025

Watford are set to appoint Edward Iordanescu as their new manager.

BBC Three Counties Radio report the Romanian is due to become the Hornets' sixth manager inside 18 months after they sacked head coach Alessio Dionisi following Saturday's 4-0 defeat at Sheffield United in his 18th game in charge.

The 48-year-old is understood to be arriving in the UK on Tuesday to sign his contract and plans to bring three members of staff with him and hopes to be in the dugout for Wednesday's Championship fixture at home to Blackburn Rovers (19:45 GMT).

Iordanescu guided Romania at Euro 2024 where they topped their group ahead of Belgium with all four sides ending level on four points from three games before a 3-0 defeat against the Netherlands in the Round of 16.

Iordanescu - whose father Anghel had three spells in charge of the Romanian national team, leading them in two World Cups and two European Championships - left his last role at Polish club Legia Warsaw in October 2025.

It was the 48-year-old's ninth club over a 15-year coaching career which has taken in Bulgarian club CSKA Sofia as well as Steaua Bucharest and Cluj among others in his homeland.

Dionisi, who departed with the Hornets in 21st, four points above the relegation zone, was only appointed in June after the departure of Ed Still, who himself lasted only three months at Vicarage Road.

Still, Javi Gracia and Paulo Pezzolano were all also given full-time contracts after Tom Cleverley left in May 2025.

The 46-year-old Italian was Watford's 12th head coach, not including interim bosses, since the end of the 2020-21 season, and leaves the Hornets searching for a 25th since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.

The club have had 57 permanent managers in their 145-year history.

#740. Who Is Adrian Williams? What to Know About Julianne Hough’s Boyfriend

Dancing With the Stars host Julianne Hough hinted she’s dating Peloton instructor Adrian Williams in a sneaky social media post Nov. 22. See everything to know about her new IRL partner.

Julianne Hough has a new partner—on and off the dancefloor.

The Dancing With The Stars host is dating Peloton instructor Adrian Williams, a source confirmed to E! News, shortly after the duo shared a sweet Instagram post Nov. 22.

Williams took the first big step in the pair’s relationship by sharing a glimpse of their bond on his Instagram Story, showing off a photo of Hough holding her dog Sunny, which Hough later reshared.

And while Hough has kept her romance out of the ballroom, she teased that she might have found a new partner back in September, four years after she and Brooks Laich finalized their divorce in 2022.

"I might not be single,” she told E! News' Justin Sylvester at the 2026 Emmys. "There's a lot to discuss off-camera.”

E! News previously reached out to reps for Hough and Williams but did not hear back.

Now that Hough has shimmied her way into a new love affair, there’s a lot to learn about her new man. Keep reading for everything to know about the Peloton instructor.

Williams has been an instructor for Peloton since 2020, cementing himself as a go-to strength and treadmill teacher, especially for those who are trying to get a workout in before the sun comes up. (Literally, his alarm goes off at 4 a.m.)

He told GQ that he teaches around 12 classes a week on top of a regimented personal fitness routine.

“My training right now is three times a week heavy weight lifting,” he told the outlet in 2021. “I do a five-by-five program. It’s pretty basic: push, pull, hinge. So I'll do deadlifts, squats, bench and overhead. One day a week I'll do either a distance run or a track situation, like a bunch of hundreds on repeat.”

Outside of the gym, he dabbles in photography, according to his Peloton biography, and appears to have an interest in luxury cars, as seen on his Instagram.

Williams is a native New Yorker, with “bold Bronx energy,” according to his Peloton biography.

Hough has been extremely mum about her latest romance, but she has shared a bit about what she was looking for before she and Williams made their relationship Instagram official.

“It's all energy-based,” Williams told E! News of what she’s looking for in a potential partner. “I don't really have a type. It's more connection, and that's it.”

And while Hough was proudly touting her single era prior to her romance with Williams, she wasn’t closing off her heart.

“I'm always looking for love,” she said, “whether it's in a romantic sense or friends.”

Of course, there was one parameter when it came to whether Williams could keep in step with her, as she previously teased to E!, her new partner needed to be “someone super hot.”

#739. Tarkowski's first Premier League red ruins Moyes' night - was it deserved?

Janelt scores stunner as Brentford beat 10-man Everton

It had been some run for Everton captain James Tarkowski.

Prior to Monday night, the defender had received 74 yellow cards in the Premier League but had never been sent off - a top-flight record.

But that run came to an end at Brentford as he was given his first red card in his 351st Premier League appearance, although the decision has attracted plenty of debate.

His dismissal crucially means he will miss Sunday's Merseyside derby against Liverpool and also ruined David Moyes' record-breaking night as he took charge of his 593rd game as Everton boss - more than anyone else in the club's history.

The 4-0 loss was also the heaviest defeat Everton have had since Moyes returned to the club at the start of last year.

Tarkowski's dismissal proved a big talking point during and after the match, with opinions split on whether he should have gone. Even Moyes wasn't sure.

He told BBC Match of the Day: "My thoughts at the time, I didn't think it was but when I've looked at it again I think his foot is high. Is there enough force for it to be a red card? Not sure about that."

James Tarkowski received his first Premier League red card

Just 15 minutes after Keane Lewis-Potter scored his second deflected strike of the evening, Everton skipper Tarkowski thundered into a challenge on Brentford's Yehor Yarmoliuk.

He won the ball but also followed through with the challenge forcefully. Initially, referee Craig Pawson deemed a foul and a yellow card was enough.

But, after an intervention from the video assistant referee (VAR) and studying the replay, Pawson changed the yellow for a red.

The Premier League match centre said on X: "After VAR review, the referee overturned the original decision of yellow card for Tarkowski for the challenge on Yarmoliuk and issued a red card for serious foul play.

"VAR: 'Point of contact is on the shin. He's got speed and intensity. Studs are high.'

"REF: 'After review, Everton No.6 commits a challenge that endangers his opponent's safety, making contact with the studs onto the shin. Cancelling the yellow card - and a red card.'"

Brentford 4-0 Everton: David Moyes post-match interview

Referees are asked to take into account several considerations for what counts as serious foul play including the speed of the challenge, its intensity, force and what degree of control there was.

But, as always, there was plenty of debate about whether it was the correct decision.

BBC Sport's football issues correspondent Dale Johnson, said: "Really not sure about this as a VAR red card.

"Yes, Tarkowski absolutely ticks the boxes for speed and intensity and leading high with studs showing.

"But the question marks are that Tarkowski made only small contact and didn't have a straight leg when he did so.

"Maybe his reputation played a part? Remember, he wrongly escaped a VAR red card against Liverpool for a challenge, which was along the same lines. He won the ball and then followed through into Alexis Mac Allister. Though that was a far stronger challenge."

BBC Radio 5 Live's - and former Blackburn Rovers striker - Chris Sutton, said on X: "Come on that's not a redâ¦ the game's gone."

Former Arsenal striker Alan Smith agreed the decision was harsh. He told Sky Sports: "Ten years ago we wouldn't have looked at it once and now we still [frame] it on the follow-through. I just can't see it.

"Only Tarkowski knows if he wanted to leave it high or if it was natural. The follow-through was just natural momentum.

"There's a bit of anger in there from Tarkowski and it's a little high but only he knows if he wanted to leave a little more on Yarmoliuk there."

Opinion was far from unanimous though, with both pundits in the Sky Sports studio adamant it was a clear red.

Former Liverpool centre-back Jamie Carragher said: "It's a red card. Tarkowski has got previous for tackles like that. He is a 90s defender, he tackles like that.

"He follows through with such force, it is excessive. You want to give him the benefit of the doubt but it's a red card."

He added: "You could argue was it a big enough mistake for VAR to get involved but I think we are splitting hairs. He doesn't need to do this."

While ex-Tottenham defender Toby Alderweireld added: "It's a red card, he knows what he is doing. 100%."

Everton fan calls Tarkoswki red card 'harsh'

Josh, Sheffield: Never a red for Tarkowski and I'm a Liverpool fan. What's he meant to do? Stop momentum. It's a good tackle and the player runs into the natural follow through

Robin, Essex: Another game ruined by VAR! Not straight leg tackle you can surely see he turned his foot around. Poor!

Rob, Manchester: These sorts of VAR decisions are making me turn off football. Why pay all that money to watch arbitrary decisions impact the game?

Lee: It is a sad day when a good tackle gets a player sent off. You slow anything down and dissect it you can find wrongs. Yellow was a bit much and the red ridiculous, we need ex players in the VAR decisions too.

Max, Oldham: What a load of nonsense the red card is. Tarkowski can't stop his momentum. VAR has ruined another game, plus what is the ref doing? He had a chance to stick with the yellow card. Another case of an official who has never played the game.

Paul, St Asaph: Tarkowski has got away with that same foul a few times. Do think he's the type of player to leave one in on purpose.

Anon: Yes it's a red - Tarkowski knows what he's doing, it's frustration and wanting to leave a bit on the player.

Chris, Chelmsford: He does it all the time at the borderline but about time he got one.

Woody, London: Lack of refinement masked as passion, classic Tarkowski tackle thereâ¦ glad to see him off.

George, Birmingham: Studs up in a tackle, he has to go. A clear red card for me.

#737. England, Northern Ireland, Scotland & Wales to host 2035 Women's World Cup

Spain beat England 1-0 to win the 2023 World Cup

England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed.

It will be the first time a football World Cup has been held in the United Kingdom since the men's tournament in 1966.

The four countries were the only bidders for the tournament, and were ratified as co-hosts at a specially arranged virtual meeting from Fifa's Zurich headquarters.

The tournament will consist of 104 matches contested by 48 teams over 39 days.

The 'All Together' bid included a proposal to use 19 venues, with 14 in England, one in Northern Ireland, two in Scotland and two in Wales.

Monday's special meeting of Fifa's Congress also approved the joint bid by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 finals, which will be the first to feature 48 teams.

The news comes on the same day the UK government announced a vision for one million more girls to play, watch or be in leadership roles in sport by the time the tournament takes place.

Hosting World Cup means decade of excitement - Weir

Fifa announces UK will host 2035 Women's World Cup

England failed to win the right to host the men's World Cups in 2006 and 2018, and a proposed UK and Ireland bid for the 2030 tournament was abandoned.

But England and Scotland hosted matches at the men's Euros in 2021, and England staged the women's European Championship in 2022, which the Lionesses won.

England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland will jointly host the men's European Championship in 2028.

Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, said: "Hosting Euro 2022 allowed us to change the game in our country, by creating a generation of aspirational role models and growing demand from women and girls to play.

"Hosting a World Cup would give us the chance to build on that across all four nations."

The English stadiums included in the 2035 bid are: Villa Park, The Amex, Ashton Gate, Elland Road, Hill Dickinson Stadium, Emirates Stadium, Selhurst Park, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Wembley, Etihad Stadium, St James' Park, the City Ground, the Stadium of Light and Old Trafford.

If Manchester United's proposed new Old Trafford stadium does not go ahead, it would still be considered in its current form.

Cardiff City Stadium and Principality Stadium are the two Welsh venues, with Easter Road in Edinburgh and Hampden Park in Glasgow in Scotland.

Northern Ireland missed out on co-hosting the men's Euros in 2028 after the UK government said in 2024 it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in time - but a redeveloped Windsor Park is set to stage matches in 2035.

A further three stadiums could be added - Birmingham's new Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham's redeveloped Racecourse Ground, and a potential new Chelsea ground - which would take the tournament to 16 cities and 22 venues.

Fifa is yet to decide whether all four co-hosts will qualify automatically.

The Principality Stadium in Cardiff is one of two Welsh venues, along with the Cardiff City Stadium

The participation of women and girls in football has risen by 2.3m since the Women's European Championship was held in England in 2022.

However, women remain significantly underrepresented in leadership positions.

Only a quarter of chief executive, chair or performance director roles in major UK sports are held by women and only 12% of sports federations are led by a female.

Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales, said: "This is a proud day for Welsh football.

"We've put forward Wrexham and Cardiff as host cities, and it's exciting to think what a World Cup could bring to both cities and the communities around them.

"In Llunio Cymru - our 10-year strategy - we've set ourselves the ambition of reaching the knockout stages in 2035. Some of the players who could take us there are learning the game at clubs across Wales today. Our job is to make sure that wherever a girl grows up in Wales, she can find a team close to home, have a coach who helps her develop and see a route to the Cymru shirt."

Irish Football Association chief executive Patrick Nelson said the event "would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country".

"Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that," he added.

Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell said hosting the tournament would be "the most significant thing to happen to the women's and girls' game in Scotland".

He added: "The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come."

Fifa's evaluation, published earlier this month, rated the bid 4.3 out of five. Its contractual framework was rated 'medium risk', and the document claimed "certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security".

That is thought to refer to a lack of agreement over a request by Fifa for tax-free status for all football-related activities.

The bid evaluation said: "The bidder has submitted an extensive set of government support documents and contractual hosting agreements, demonstrating the commitment of the relevant authorities and stakeholders.

"However, certain government guarantees, particularly those relating to safety and security and tax, contain certain qualifications which have been duly noted in the legal evaluation.

"While certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion, the bidder's proactive engagement with Fifa and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding issues."
