#689. 100 Years of Music at Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, For ‘An Audience Aged 1 to 100’

"It's your Thanksgiving Day playlist, it's your annual yearbook," Will Coss of Macy's Studios tells Billboard of booking artists over a century of parades.

No holiday tradition sums up America quite like the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

For more than a century now, the annual extravaganza has wound its way from Manhattan’s Upper West Side through Midtown Manhattan and across Herald Square to the famous star outside the historic Macy’s flagship store on 34th Street.

Filled with giant balloons, colorful floats, clowns, musical performances, squads of cheerleaders and marching bands, the parade has become nothing short of a holiday institution. In fact, the event has taken place every year since 1924, with the exception of just two years when it was put on pause during World War II.

As it’s grown, the parade has also reached far beyond the streets of New York City, with NBC broadcasting all the fun, music and magic live coast to coast since the late 1950s. In any given household, odds are, the parade will be on the television come Thanksgiving morning, providing a cozy and familiar tradition as turkeys are basted, potatoes are mashed and finishing touches are put on each pie.

Macy’s annual parade has become an integral, often cherished part of the day, as families, friends and loved ones gather around kitchen tables. For many parade lovers, the march through Manhattan heralds the official start of the holiday season, thanks to Tom Turkey’s ever-trusty appearance at the head of the parade and Santa’s arrival in his giant sleigh signaling the grand finale.

Remarkably, this year’s holiday marks the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, which is set to air live on NBC, Peacock and Telemundo on Thursday morning (Nov. 26) from 8:30 a.m. to noon ET.

Ahead of the telecast, take a march down memory lane for a special look at the parade’s humble beginnings, its history of can’t-miss musical performances, and what fans can expect from this year’s historic centennial celebration.

In November 1924, the very first Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was actually dreamed up by a group of European immigrants working at the department store after their arrival in the Big Apple. Donning colorful costumes, the Macy’s employees based the original incarnation on parades held in their respective home countries across the Atlantic.

They even borrowed lions, elephants and bears from the Central Park Zoo that first year as part of the parade’s entertainment — though traipsing wild animals across Herald Square was quickly deemed a safety hazard and the large mammals stayed home in the zoo in subsequent years.

Thanks to puppetry pioneer Tony Sarg, balloons soon replaced live animals as the most famous element of the parade. Music has also always been a key part of the event, with marching bands entertaining crowds with live music from the parade’s earliest days. By 1958, celebrity performers were added to the lineup to provide even more entertainment value, with Benny Goodman’s sextet traditionally considered the first famous act to join the parade in 1958.

In the decades since, performing at the parade on Thanksgiving morning has been a bucket-list item for artists of all kinds — from country stars and crooners to rappers, boy bands and American Idol winners — singing on floats and lighting up the stage on 34th Street.

Legends like Dolly Parton, Diana Ross and Tony Bennett have delighted paradegoers numerous times across multiple decades. The country icon made her parade debut back in 1975 by performing “Love Is Like a Butterfly” on the famed Tom Turkey float; she’d make return visits in 2007 and 2020. Four years after Parton’s first appearance, Ross rode the Big Apple float and made good on her self-appointed nickname by performing “The Boss.” Nearly four decades later, the Queen of Motown returned to sing “Wonderful Christmastime” in 2018, flanked by her famous family members, including Tracee Ellis-Ross, Evan Ross and Ashlee Simpson.

As for Bennett, his four appearances range from 1962, when he performed “I Left My Heart in San Francisco” ahead of a headlining show at Carnegie Hall, to 2016, when he rang in his 90th birthday alongside the parade’s 90th anniversary.

In 2022, Mariah Carey graced Herald Square with her presence for the first time, after previously performing on a float in 2015. In the lead-up to Santa Claus’ arrival, the unequivocal Queen of Christmas closed out the parade with a festive performance of “All I Want for Christmas Is You” — complete with bejeweled tiara, glamorous red gown and a wintry parasol in hand.

Given the magnitude of the event, selecting acts each year for every float and onstage performance is a feat akin to booking an entire multi-stage music festival, except it also happens to be moving through the biggest city in the country.

“It is a massive undertaking,” Will Coss, vice president and head of Macy’s Studios, tells Billboard. “Every one of our floats is a moving stage, it is a theatrical performance. … Our north star when we’re booking the parade is really to ensure that we have best in class: the best artists, the best performers. But we also want to ensure that we’re appealing to the wide range of our audience. We like to say we have an audience aged 1 to 100.”

The parade has also become an early tried-and-true proving ground for artists who’ve gone on to become global superstars. Backstreet Boys, *NSYNC and Christina Aguilera all performed in front of millions of people at the parade in the early days of the teen pop boom from 1997 to 1999, and a then-17-year-old Rihanna brought her Caribbean roots to the 2005 installment with a performance of her debut single “Pon de Replay.”

The Jonas Brothers made appearances in both 2006 and 2007, rocking out to “Year 3000” and “S.O.S.” in back-to-back performances pre-dating their debut as Disney Channel heartthrobs in 2008’s Camp Rock. The siblings’ second time at the parade was marred by a literal S.O.S., however, when a mix-up left them stranded, musically speaking, aboard the Build-A-Bear Workshop float for much of the route.

“We couldn’t find our instruments,” Joe Jonas recalled years later in a 2011 TV special commemorating the parade’s 85th anniversary. “We thought they would be on [the float]. We’re literally pulling out to start and we don’t have our microphones, our instruments or anything.” (Only after a good Samaritan lent them a couple of spare guitars and a tambourine were Kevin, Nick and Joe able to perform “S.O.S.” upon arriving in Herald Square.)

A few years later, Ariana Grande covered “Last Christmas” aboard the Dora the Explorer float just weeks after releasing her debut album Yours Truly in 2013. And less than a decade before making history at the 2026 Super Bowl halftime show, Bad Bunny made a bold step into mainstream pop culture consciousness by performing his X 100pre-era single “Estamos Bien” surrounded by kids on the Sour Patch Kids float. (A few years later, Benito also inspired his own novelty balloon based on the artwork of his 2022 No. 1 album Un Verano Sin Ti.)

To the executives who spend all year planning the parade’s lineup, the importance of booking emerging talent is twofold. “When we talk to artists, wherever they are in their career, everyone’s got a story, everyone’s got a connection [to the parade],” Coss says. “I think this is one of those moments, this is one of those bucket-list moments to check off and to say, ‘I’ve arrived!’”

“There’s no bigger platform in the calendar year for families than the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade,” adds Jen Neal, NBCUniversal’s evp of Live Events & Specials. “In terms of the entertainment show, it is the largest audience that reaches the most people in the annual year. For artists to get the platform and reach audiences that are co-viewing with family, it’s safe and special. It brings people together, so from an artist perspective, the scale is unparalleled. So it’s a perfect launching point.”

Occasionally, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade also provides the perfect stage for a history-making moment. Just last year, Macy’s and NBC execs were hard at work planning the 99th parade as Netflix’s KPop Demon Hunters exploded into a global phenomenon.

“We were tracking the pulse and the excitement and the rise of that franchise as it was happening in real time,” Coss says. With just weeks to go, they made the relative last-minute decision to make magic happen, commissioning a Derpy balloon and inviting EJAE, Audrey Nuna and REI AMI — the singing voices of HUNTR/X — to make their parade debut with a performance of “Golden.”

Coss saw the KPop Demon Hunters performance as “an opportunity to be on the pulse of culture” and create the kind of year-defining moment that corresponds with the entire ethos behind the parade’s annual roster of performers.

“It’s your Thanksgiving Day playlist, it’s your annual yearbook, your kind of year in review,” he says. “Those are the filters that we use as we’re thinking about artists.”

Elsewhere, unexpected moments of delight are bound to happen once NBC’s cameras start rolling. Another surprise occurred last year when Busta Rhymes was joined by the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles for a high-octane, career-spanning medley that included “Pass the Courvoisier Part II,” “Break Ya Neck,” “Look at Me Now” and “Put Your Hands Where My Eyes Could See.”

“That profile shot of the Turtle going in with Busta, that went viral and was one of the most clicked and talked about moments [from 2025],” Coss says. “That’s the beauty and the spirit of the parade, you never know where that breakout moment’s gonna happen.”

While most parades take roughly 18 months to plan and execute, this year’s centennial celebration has been in the works for the last five years.

The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade promises to combine nostalgic magic and fan-favorite traditions families have come to love with bigger spectacle and special nods to the parade’s century-long history.

For starters, this year’s parade will feature 100 different balloons — nearly double the 50 to 60 helium giants on display in a typical year. Brand-new additions include cultural icons like Bluey, Hello Kitty and Joe Cool as well as the long-awaited return of the beloved characters like Sonic the Hedgehog, Popeye, Olive Oyl and Underdog. (“Since my first day in this position, all the fans and volunteers I meet are always asking, ‘When’s Underdog coming back? When’s Underdog coming back?’” Coss says with a laugh.)

The parade will also honor the pioneering work of its original balloon innovator with Tony Sarg’s Marionette Theater, a brand-new float featuring classic balloon creatures like Morton the Nantucket Sea Dragon, Jerry the Pig and the Crying Baby.

Meanwhile, the line-up of performers is star-studded as ever, with RAYE set to open the parade fresh off earning a leading 11 Grammy nominations. Additional artists already confirmed to appear include Billboard chart-toppers Teddy Swims and Megan Moroney as well as Jamie Miller, Billboard’s November 2026 Chartbreaker, along with the solo return of EJAE.

Other acts on the lineup: RIIZE, Queen Latifah, Jimmy Fallon and The Roots, JoJo, Keke Palmer, Smash Mouth, Mckenna Grace, DEVO, the Indigo Girls, Natasha Bedingfield, Feid, Icona Pop, Wyclef Jean and more. Broadway star Megan Hilty will lead a special musical tribute to Dolly Parton, with more performers expected to be announced ahead of Thanksgiving day.

And though viewers can expect this year’s 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to be grander and better than ever before, the goal remains the same: to serve up a feast of nostalgia and holiday magic for families across America.

“It comes down to the opportunity to create memories,” Coss says. “We all remember where we were, either that cold morning on Thanksgiving or that rainy morning on Thanksgiving if you’re watching it in person. Or the time Dad burned the turkey on Thanksgiving and the parade was on in the background. We take great pride in creating those moments that connect us all together.”

#688. Steven Hack, Broadway Star and American Horror Story Actor, Dead at 68

Broadway star Steven Hack—also known for roles on shows like Seinfeld, General Hospital and American Horror Story—has died at age 68.

A bright light in Hollywood has gone dim.

Broadway star Steven Hack, who also had minor roles in American Horror Story and Seinfeld, has died after suffering a medical emergency, Los Angeles’ Interact Theatre Company confirmed. He was 68.

“It is with great sadness that we share the news that Steven Hack, a founding member of Interact Theatre Company, recently passed away at home following a sudden and unexpected cardiac event,” the company wrote in a recent statement shared to Instagram. “Steven was a gifted and versatile performer, a superb graphic artist, and a cherished member of our artistic family.”

Hack died of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, according to the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner, a condition caused by plaque buildup in the arterial walls, per the America Heart Association.

“His creativity and talent helped shape Interact in its earliest years,” the statement continued, “and his artistry, humor, warmth, and generous spirit enriched everything he touched.”

Hack was born in St. Louis in 1958 before going on to study at the California Institute of the Arts and the American Academy of Dramatic Arts.

“Steven took great pride in his early career as a Broadway dancer, which included performing in the original production of CATS and touring with A Chorus Line,” Interact Theatre Company noted. “Here in Los Angeles, he went on to work extensively in film, television, and commercials.”

In fact, he made his screen debut as one of the teenage dancers in the 1978 film Grease before landing roles in other films like Fantastic Four, Thor: The Dark World and The Happytime Murders.

He also dominated the small screen with credits in American Horror Story: 1984, Marvel’s Agent Carter, Criminal Minds, The Newsroom, Days of Our Lives, The West Wing, Scrubs, General Hospital, Seinfeld and so many more.

“As we remember Steven, we celebrate not only his many contributions to our company, but also the joy of knowing and working with him,” Interact Theatre Company wrote. “He will always hold a special place in Interact’s history and in the hearts of those who knew him.”

They expressed hope that Hack’s "memory be a blessing,” adding, "We extend our heartfelt condolences to his family, friends, and all who loved him.”

#687. Anuel AA Blames Delayed Bogotá Show on Team Member’s ‘Big Mistake,’ Promises Free Makeup Concert

The Puerto Rican artist said a scheduling error left him arriving more than two hours late and performing for just 50 minutes.

Anuel AA has promised to return to Bogotá, Colombia, for a free concert after facing backlash over his Saturday (Nov. 21) performance at Vive Claro. The Puerto Rican rapper took the stage more than two hours after the scheduled start time and performed for just 50 minutes.

In a statement shared on his Instagram Stories Monday (Nov. 23), Anuel said he would announce details of the complimentary show when he announces his forthcoming Real Hasta La Muerte 2 tour.

“Bogotá, for those who are truly my fans, when I announce the Real Hasta La Muerte 2 tour, I’ll announce the free concert to make up for what happened and do things right,” he wrote in Spanish. “There was a really big mistake made by one person on my team, and that’s why I arrived so late and only sang for 50 minutes.”

Anuel explained that his itinerary listed the concert as a festival, and that he had been told his set would begin at 11:30 p.m. The rapper also said that, by the time he arrived at the stadium, he was told everything was fine. He claimed he cut his performance short because the police threatened to shut off the sound system.

“If it were up to me, I wouldn’t have performed. I would have had the fans’ money refunded and rescheduled the date,” he added. He said the consequences within his company would be proportional to the scale of the mistake.

The shortened set sparked outrage among concertgoers. Videos circulating on social media appeared to show attendees throwing chairs and bottles, as well as altercations in the stands. Some fans have since demanded refunds.

The controversy follows the postponement of Anuel’s Nov. 22 concert in the Medellín metropolitan area until 2027 due to scheduling adjustments, leaving Bogotá as his only Colombian tour stop this year.

AME Concerts and Iguana Producciones were identified as the organizers. Neither has issued a statement, according to Colombian outlet Caracol Radio.

Anuel has yet to announce a date or venue for the free concert, or say whether admission will be reserved for those who purchased tickets to Saturday’s show.

#686. Mary J. Blige Ruling, Cher Sonny Bono Lawsuit, Julio Iglesias Case & More Top Music Law News

In this week's Legal Beat newsletter, a big ruling on "Real Love," Cher's battle with Sonny's widow, an abuse probe for Julio Iglesias and much more.

THE BIG STORY: Mary J. Blige won a court ruling this week that was more than 50 years in the making —and one that offers a history lesson on both hip-hop and music law.

When Blige released her song “Real Love” in 1992, it featured elements of “Impeach the President” by The Honey Drippers — a 1973 protest funk song that was widely sampled in the early days of rap and has made appearances in tracks by Run-DMC, Dr. Dre, LL Cool J and, more recently, Doja Cat. “Impeach” was so ubiquitous that Blige seems to have used it indirectly, via a direct sample of a different 1987 hip-hop track that had sampled it.

Decades later, in 2024, a label called Tuff City Records, which owns the famous sample, took UMG to court over it. And the lawsuit revealed that a strange situation had played out behind the scenes: Apparently, UMG’s recorded music unit quickly settled and agreed to pay for the sample, but its publishing unit refused to do so, choosing instead to fight it out in court over whether it also had to pay.

That weird situation highlights an important distinction in music law: While courts have long ruled that direct sampling of a copyrighted sound recording requires a license for any use no matter how insignificant, the rules for interpolating a copyrighted musical composition are far less clear-cut.

Case in point: Despite the use of the sample of the recording, a judge sided with UMG last year on the composition, dismissing Tuff City’s case on the grounds that “the songs do not sound the same.” And in a new ruling this week, a federal appeals court affirmed that decision, ruling that Blige’s song was simply not similar enough to The Honey Drippers’ to count as infringement of the underlying music.

What about that history lesson? Well, back in 1991, Tuff City filed another case over “Impeach the President,” that time suing Sony Music for allegedly featuring it on two LL Cool J tracks. At the time, uncleared sampling was widely accepted in hip-hop, but a 1992 New York Times article warned that Tuff City’s lawsuit could change all that.

The case settled, but the warnings about sampling eventually proved accurate. Federal courts later gradually ruled that any amount of sampling of sound recordings counts as copyright infringement, including a famous ruling that sternly warned: “Get a license or do not sample.” And as a result, labels and artists today clear almost all direct samples and remove them if they cannot.

That abundance of caution has often led to also paying for the underlying composition to the same track — precisely what UMG refused to do here. Will the “Real Love” ruling embolden other artists and labels to do the same?

Perhaps the history on that one is still being written.

— Members of the Americana band The Mavericks said they were “saddened” by a lawsuit filed by the widow of late frontman Raul Malo seeking to ban them from using the band’s name.

— Speaking of samples: Travis Scott, Don Toliver and others members of JACKBOYS were hit with a copyright lawsuit over an alleged sample in their 2019 track “What To Do?”

— A grand jury declined to bring charges against Boosie Badazz over an alleged violent altercation at a Houston nightclub this year — though the rapper’s legal troubles are not yet over.

— Summer Walker fired back with a countersuit against Interscope Records amid their broader fight over her record deal, accusing the UMG label of misusing her intellectual property.

— 50 Cent won a ruling dismissing a lawsuit that claimed he threatened and harassed a former exec at his company, but she’s likely going to refile the case and continue the fight.

#685. Pakistani astronaut to become first foreign visitor to China’s space station

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Three astronauts will launch aboard China’s Shenzhou-24 spacecraft.Credit: Xinhua/Shutterstock

For the first time, China will send a foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station.

Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a Pakistani military pilot, is expected to travel to Tiangong on 25 November aboard China’s Shenzhou-24 spacecraft, alongside two Chinese astronauts, known as ‘taikonauts’.

“My first [flight] not only represents myself, but also my country,” Ali told reporters in Mandarin on 24 November at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China. Ali has been training intensively in Beijing for the past seven months, including learning Mandarin. He said that he carried “the dream of 250 million Pakistani people” when he entered the training centre.

Sending an astronaut to space is “a huge step” for Pakistan’s space aspirations, says Wajiha Iqbal, a lunar scientist at the University of Münster in Germany. The partnership enables Pakistan to “do great science in space”, she adds.

The mission is also a milestone for China’s space programme. The country’s expanding capabilities now allow it to offer international partners opportunities that few countries can provide on their own, says Yuxuan Jia, who researches China’s foreign policy at the Center for China and Globalization, a think tank in Beijing. The launch signals China’s “aspirations to become a top space power”, Jia says.

Shenzhou-24 is expected to be carried into a low-Earth orbit by China’s Long March-2F rocket, which is scheduled to launch from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre at 08:18am local time on 25 November, said Zhang Jingbo, a spokesperson of the China Manned Space Programme, at a press conference on 24 November. Shenzhou-24 is expected to automatically dock with Tiangong (which translates as ‘heavenly palace’) around 3.5 hours after reaching orbit.

Ali will stay on Tiangong for about a week before returning to Earth with two of the three taikonauts currently on the station.

China’s successful launch of Mars mission seals global era in deep-space exploration

China’s successful launch of Mars mission seals global era in deep-space exploration

Ali will board Shenzhou-24 as a payload specialist responsible mainly for scientific experiments rather than operating the spacecraft. The mission aims to host four biotechnology experiments developed by universities in Pakistan, Amer Gilani, an official at Pakistan’s space agency told newswire Reuters in September. Details about the research have not yet been made public.

According to Zhang, one goal of this mission is to establish a study of how the human body adapts to space flight. Zhu Yangzhu, an astronaut who entered Tiangong in May, will remain aboard the space station for another six months to allow for this experiment to take place, Zhang said.

Astronauts Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, Wu Yi and Tang Hongbo will travel to China's space station the Tiangong.Credit: CCTV+/VCG via Getty

#681. Netflix Buys Radford Studio Lot for $380 Million

The purchase gives the entertainment giant ownership of a major Los Angeles production campus.

Netflix is buying Radford Studio Center for $380 million, taking ownership of one of Hollywood’s most storied production lots as the entertainment giant expands its physical footprint in Los Angeles.

The deal, which is expected to close on Tuesday, follows an auction during which the property’s lender took back the property after Hackman Capital Partners defaulted on its mortgage amid historically low production levels in the region. Netflix reached an agreement with the Goldman Sachs-led lender to acquire the lot.

The $380 million price point is roughly 20 percent of the $1.85 billion Hackman paid for Radford in 2021, a massive repricing of a legacy Hollywood lot and indicative of the flight of filming away from Los Angeles and California. Related Stories Business Bela Bajaria Calls Time at Netflix a "Fun Chapter" as She Teases Rest and "Conversations" in First Remarks on Exit Movies Sadie Sandler to Star in Netflix Horror Movie 'Malibu' From Vertigo, Happy Madison (Exclusive)

After it took over the property, Goldman handled the foreclosure to facilitate a sale. As part of the deal, Netflix paid the so-called mansion tax, which imposes a 5.5 percent levy for properties valued above $10.9 million, says a person familiar with the sale.

As part of the deal, Netflix has pacted with Louis Dargenzio’s rising studio services firm Zello, contracting with its entertainment advisory division ZVantage to manage the transition as well as partnering with Dargenzio’s production equipment provider Cinelease to provide services.

The purchase will shake up Netflix’s production pipeline in L.A. For years, it’s been the anchor tenant at Sunset Studios while also filming at Raleigh Studios. With the 55-acre shooting campus, the company could consolidate production scattered across the region while cutting costs associated with renting.

In a memo to staff, Netflix said that it purchased Radford to “strengthen our investment in Los Angeles and California.”

“This city is home to us,” it said. “We’re excited to keep investing here and finding more ways to entertain the world, while supporting the writers, builders, electricians, drivers, designers, and talent who make L.A., California, and the entertainment industry so special.”

Since 2018, Netflix has filmed more than 300 movies and TV shows — including The Rip, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth and GLOW — primarily in L.A. More than 45 came this year as the company says it plans to deepens its roots in the region.

“There’s still a long way to go, but we are hopeful that with the partnership of the State of California and the City of Los Angeles, this will be the start of a meaningful new investment in California’s film industry,” it said in the memo.

The deal could also impact Netflix’s office operations, though the company has no changes in mind in the short-term. It leases over 700,000 square feet across the ICON, EPIC and CUE buildings at Sunset Studios. Those leases are scheduled to expire in 2031.

#680. Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion

The Kremlin is reportedly calling on NATO to withdraw from large parts of Eastern Europe. What this would mean for the security of millions of Europeans — and what lies behind Russia's plan.

During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.

Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.

The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.

According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave, but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.

A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.

In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.

"Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well."

The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.

In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.

For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.

As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.

Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.

During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.

Their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.

In the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.

In the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.

Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.

Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.

So far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.

This article was originally published in German.

#679. 5 Things to Know About Anuel AA Ahead of His ‘RHLM2’ Album Release

From his being a hopeless romantic to his bromance with Fuerza Regida's JOP, see the list of things we learned about Anuel AA from his recent 'Billboard' interview below.

Anuel AA is finally releasing his highly-anticipated new album, RHLM2, on his birthday, Nov. 26.

The forthcoming set, which is a follow-up to his debut album Real Hasta La Muerte released in 2018, will have tracks that blend trap and reggaetón, and marks a return to his origins, as he exclusively revealed during the exclusive Superstar Q&A and Premiere Party at Billboard Latin Music Week in October.

During the 45-minute conversation, moderated by Leila Cobo, Billboard’s co-chief content officer, he also teased many of the set’s songs including its new single “Se tocó el totico con mi glock.” “This trap song is one for the streets, for the bebesitas — it’s that kind of song,” he said then. “It’s one of my favorites. It was a tough decision to include it, though writing it wasn’t difficult at all.”

Though it’s taken him nearly 10 years to release the sequel to RHLM — which debuted at No. 1 on Top Latin Albums in July 2018—the Puerto Rican artist has released other promising albums in between including: Emmanuel (2020) and Las Leyendas Nunca Mueren (2021), both of which also hit No. 1 on the chart.

On Friday (Nov. 20), the artist revealed the cover art and release date for RHLM2 on his Instagram account, assuring in the caption: “I poured my heart and soul into this album for everyone who believes in me and stays loyal no matter what… This album means the world to me.”

Ahead of the album’s release on Thanksgiving (Nov. 26), Billboard revisits the artist’s recent exclusive Billboard News interview with Cobo and breaks down five things we learned:

If his past public relationships that included Karol G and Yailin La Más Viral are any indication, Anuel AA is a hopeless romantic. In the Billboard News interview, the Puerto Rican artist admitted that he’s always falling in love, a sentiment that’s reflected in his new music today.

“You have to cater to all kinds of fans. Sometimes I’m with friends who play nothing but romantic songs, and they’re all serious and bored… some people have dead hearts; they need to fall in love more in life. I fall in love every single day,” he said.

Furthermore, he joked about Karol G — whom he dated from 2018 to 2021 — asking her to unblock him from social media. “Why live with so much hatred? I’m not trying to bother her, but she needs to unblock me! We should live life in peace. Someone ought to make a movie about my love life — it would sell really well; it would be amazing,” he expressed.

Anuel opened up about his mental health, remembering when he was underweight and unhealthy just two years ago. “I was going through hell… I watch those videos and say, ‘Thank God I was able to get out of there,'” he said of the challenging times he faced. “When you’re not yourself, you don’t realize it until certain people talk to you. There was a time when I would look in the mirror and not recognize the person staring back. I didn’t know if I would ever come back from that, but with God in your heart, you have to look at yourself, reflect, and accept that you made a mistake. You can’t live in denial. The first step is to see your mistake, accept it, and learn how to ensure it never happens again.”

Anuel and his longtime music viral, Cosculluela, are finally in good terms, according to the trap artist. The two Puerto Rican artists are popularly known for their tiraera or diss tracks to each other. Notably, in 2018, Anuel recorded a nearly nine-minute “tiraera” for Coscu called “Intocable,” which caused him the cancellation of his first-ever concert in Puerto Rico due to its explicit and offensive lyrics. But those moments are now long in the past. “Despite these long-standing problems, thank God we’ve taken a big step forward in our relationship, moved past all that negativity, and are now working together,” Anuel noted.

In addition to RHLM2, Anuel plans to drop an all-corridos album that he worked on in Mexico, with Mexican producers, songwriters and artists. Among his many collaborators is Fuerza Regida’s frontman JOP, whom has become a close friend of his. “There will be songs produced by Fuerza Regida,” he explained. “I’m talking with Jesus, who is helping me out with several tracks. He’s like a brother to me; we share a lot and have a great relationship.”

Anuel and JOP have already released three tracks together: “Cuando No Era Cantante RMX,” “Lokita,” and “Hay Con Que.” The former of the three was a two-time finalist at the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards, including for Global 200 Latin Song of the Year.

During the Billboard News interview with Leila Cobo, Anuel revealed that he’s producing a festival called Real Hasta La Muerte, where he will count with the support of many artists. His plans are to inaugurate the festival in 2027 in Spain — with the hopes of moving it to different countries, including Mexico, Colombia, America and Chile.

#678. The Pulitzer-Winning Play ‘Purpose’ Finally Came to Los Angeles. But That Doesn’t Mean It’s Gone Hollywood.

Branden Jacobs-Jenkins reunites the entire company, including Kara Young and director Phylicia Rashad, for a sold-out run at the Geffen Playhouse.

Branden Jacobs-Jenkins is, famously, a tinkerer. His plays go through long, thoughtful development processes. He first wrote Appropriate a decade before it became the 2024 Tony Award-winning play starring Sarah Paulson. His next work, Purpose, went through a nuanced workshop with the actors before it premiered at the Steppenwolf Theatre in Chicago; the company finalized the ending one day before the first performance. “They were walking on stage with pages in hand, that’s how fresh it was,” says Jacobs-Jenkins. “But they say the great writers all rewrite — Arthur Miller was rewriting his plays at the end of his life. Shakespeare obviously was rewriting King Lear over and over again.” Related Stories Lifestyle 'The Comedy About Spies' to Open on Broadway This Spring Lifestyle 'Birthright,' About Differing Attitudes on Israel, Set For Broadway

Director Phylicia Rashad is quick to point out that she sees Jacobs-Jenkins’ process as a gift, noting how rare it is for a company to have success access to the playwright during rehearsals. “I’ve only had this experience once before, with August Wilson and Gem of the Ocean,” she says. “The first production I did was here in Los Angeles at the Mark Taper forum, and then it went to the Huntington in Boston and eventually to Broadway — he continued to refine that play until we opened on Broadway, and I loved it.” Plus, she adds of Jacobs-Jenkins, “You cannot tell a playwright, this genius, ‘You have got to have this by three o’clock tomorrow.’ That doesn’t work.”

Purpose eventually transferred to Broadway, where it won best play and best performance by an actress in a featured role (for Kara Young), as well as the 2025 Pulitzer Prize for drama. But Jacobs-Jenkins says that despite the accolades he still hopes to polish it until the bitter end. “Every time I hear the play I think: I want to change this or that,” he laughs.

The storied stage play, which centers on a politically dynastic Black family (not entirely unlike that of the Reverend Jesse Jackson) during a dinner welcoming their eldest home from his white collar crime prison stint, is now in the midst of a revival at Los Angeles’ Geffen Playhouse. The entire Broadway cast, along with Rashad, reunited for the L.A. run, an occasion that proved both historic and also tempting for a playwright who loves the chance to revisit his work. “I actually felt a lot of pressure to leave it alone, because so many people want to see the Broadway production,” he says. “So I can’t just be out here messing with the thing. I don’t want to rock the boat.”

Here, Jacobs-Jenkins tells THR about what it’s like to bring a piece of theater to a famously screen-forward town.

When you wrote Purpose, did you imagine it would have as much success as it did?

That’s the thing, is that I really try to keep myself in check because I can get a little wild. I try to fight the fire right in front of me. I had this commission from the Steppenwolf Theater Company to write a play, and Alana Arenas is this incredible actor at the company and honestly my wildest dream was to bring her to Broadway. She plays Morgan in Purpose, and she’s one of those people that if you know her you’re obsessed with her. So I was like, I’m about to bring her to New York. And I got to do that, which is crazy. But the truth is I wanted to make something with people I like. And for whatever reason, whenever I do something with that in mind, it does keep going. If I’m launching something with some ambition, it’s always falling apart, but if a project starts with the people they go the furthest. I’ve learned that lesson.

Purpose first played for audiences in Chicago, and then New York. Does it feel at all formidable to come to an industry town?

I’ve had some great experiences in L.A. with theater, honestly. My play Gloria happened here and did pretty well. And Appropriate played at the Mark Taper Forum. It’s not a theater town, but it is an actor town. Anytime I’ve done a show here, the cast has been absolutely incredible. The audiences weren’t necessarily the most full, but the people who were there were theatergoers. For me, theater has to be a celebration of the actor. These people go out there, they’re not hiding behind a cut, they’re not hiding behind coverage. They’re like athletes and they’re telling you a story in real time without a break. In Chicago, audiences are very sophisticated, they have a high bar for writing because they’re the city of David Mamet, they’re the city of Tracy Letts. L.A. has a similar vibe, but also… I don’t know how to go down this road though, I’m not trying to say anything spicy. I would say there can be a dismissiveness of theater, because when you see the kind of capital that moves through television and film, the company town energy can take over. Even though theater could be the most impactful, powerful experience of your life, nobody is counting box office.

How much pressure do you feel towards writing screenplays or putting your stage work up for adaptation?

I would never adapt my own plays to movies or film, but I do love those mediums and I’ve dabbled in both with varying degrees of success. Like most playwrights, I’ve been feeding myself with some screen work for quite some time now. I’m a proud member of the WGA-East. But I know that I can do whatever I want in a play and I don’t have to beg some executive to let me do. I never have to ask for permission to execute my ideas. That freedom is so necessary to me as an artist. It’s funny, some of the most powerful directors and showrunners I know have said they’re jealous of my work and I’m like, what the fuck are you talking about? But it’s because we’re all just writers who want to be able to execute our visions — and there’s less red tape in the theater.

But you could also pass off the adapting, and the dealing with red tape, to someone else…

I think a lot of hit plays and musicals that have been turned into movies and they just don’t hit the same way. And I don’t want to get blamed for that. So if somebody else came along trying to do it, I’m here to support them. If they win, I win. Tennessee Williams never adapted his own scripts — the smartest thing he did was be like, I’m going to sit back and take this check, but I hope y’all have a good time. That being said, I feel like people do make the mistake of thinking these forms are more similar than they are. The pleasures are very different.

You know they’re developing The Invite for Broadway, right?

Did no one learn anything from Dog Day Afternoon? Why would someone pay a premium to see a play when they can go home and see the movie that they already know is really good. I mean, let me stop. I should not talk smack about it, but it does make me think, what? I would love it if they would just bankroll a new play. There have been several hit movies and TV shows lately that people have said, oh it’s so good, it’s like a play. Like Adolescence, when everyone was like, “Oh my God, they’re acting in real time.” And people who do plays are like, “Yeah we do that every night. What are you guys freaking out about?” Come see a play. If your vibe is two couples in an apartment, I have so many good plays for you.

We’ve been developing Grass for two years, we had a great workshop last September, and we start rehearsals in two months. We just got a cast together, and it’s going to star Daniel Kaluuya.

I’m sure you saw his hit on the local Oregon news during the FAA shutdown?

I got so many texts about him. He has responsibilities, he was on his way somewhere special, okay? (Laughs.) I’m glad he’s back on the news for whatever reasons.

#676. Jennifer Lawrence Cheekily Pushes Back on Eyelid Plastic Surgery Rumor

Jennifer Lawrence responded to speculation that she underwent upper eyelid surgery, stoked by The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, as she promoted her haircare line using her signature humor.

Jennifer Lawrence isn't letting speculation cloud her vision.

The Hunger Games star poked fun at theories that she'd recently undergone an eyelid surgery commonly referred to as an upper bleph, which have gained traction online since her return to the big screen for Sunrise on the Reaping.

Responding to her makeup artist Shayna Gold sharing a special delivery of Lawrence's new haircare line, Mes, the actress wrote on Instagram Stories Nov. 23, "iykyk she's the one who did my bleph."

The 36-year-old's one-liner referred to an upper blepharoplasty, a procedure that reconstructs the upper eyelid area, including the skin, socket and fat surrounding the eyelid. According to the National Institutes of Health, it's one of the most common operations done to the face.

Her comment appeared to shut down fan rumors—which were fueled by Gold's recent post of a photoshoot where she styled Lawrence's makeup—that she had elective plastic surgery to reduce her hooded lids. While the Red Sparrow actress didn't deny receiving the procedure outright, her cheeky response hinted that her new appearance is all thanks to makeup instead.

And when it comes to cosmetic alterations, the Oscar winner has previously divulged her latest beauty upgrades, including her decision to receive breast implants this year.

"They’re new," she told Andy Cohen on WWHL, adding of her cup size, "It’s a full C, I think. It’s the same size that they were."

But the beauty founder is prioritizing the balance between sipping from the fountain of youth and protecting her ability to perform her craft.

"I can’t really get very much done," Lawrence told Vogue in September. "I need to have movement in my face—I get baby Botox, but I can't do a lot. If my skin is going to be a little saggier than I would like, at least it looks dewy and pretty."

As such, Lawrence—mom to two kids with husband of seven years Cooke Maroney—explained she is hesitant to partake in facial fat transfers, though she did name what procedure interested her most.

"I would love to have a buccal fat removal. I can’t because everybody would know, but just know that I want that," she said, noting, "I want to continue to watch and see what happens, but I don’t know about that."

Curious about what stars have said no to a nip and tuck? For more celebrities who have spoken out against plastic surgery, read on...

The Euphoria actress confirmed in December 2025 that she hasn't had a boob job.

As costar Amanda Seyfried told her during Vanity Fair's Lie Detector Test, “There’s been a question on everybody’s minds recently, and I just have to ask, are your boobs real?”

“Yes,” Sydney responded. “I’ve never gotten any work done anywhere.”

She shared in December 2025 that she's never gotten filler.

“As you are going along in your journey, I don’t think that you should overdo it with surgery, filler, Botox,” she told People. “You don’t need to do too much. Take it easy. Less is always better."

Travis Barker and ex Shanna Moakler's daughter has been open about her use of lip fillers but denies having cosmetic surgery.

In February 2024, she shared photos of herself wearing a bikini on Instagram, to which a user commented, "This child has done alot of cosmetic surgery @ a very young age, I hope she doesn't over do it! She looks good now!"

The rapper responded, "I really appreciate the love! I'm natural, besides my lips, accept the fact I'm naturally beautiful."

The Twilight alum told Harper's Bazaar U.K. in 2015 she will "never" get plastic surgery, adding, "I am so freaked out by the idea of doing anything. And maybe that's completely arrogant but I don't want to change anything about myself. I think the women who do are losing their minds. It's vandalism."

The Devil Wears Prada star told Good Housekeeping in 2008. "You have to embrace getting older. Life is precious, and when you've lost a lot of people, you realize each day is a gift."

The "God's Plan" rapper shut down rumors in September 2025 that he had plastic surgery to make his abs more defined, explaining the fan speculation was a result of using a photo editing app.

"I came from the gym, I was sweaty in that pic," he said during an episode of Bobbi Althoff’s Not This Again podcast. "Maybe I heightened the saturation or something on it."

He added, "I think I hit it too hard. They don't look like that."

While Drake noted that people go under the knife "all the time," he isn’t one of them.

"People also say that I got a BBL," he continued, referencing the popular Brazilian Butt Lift procedure. "They call me 'BBL Drizzy.'"

The supermodel opened up about why she's all about embracing her skin at every age.

"This is a 58 year old face without fillers, Botox or surgery in good light with professional gorgeous makeup," she wrote in an August 2023 Instagram caption. "I have chosen not to put anything 'into' my face."

She continued, "Some days, I like it. I feel like my face has gained character even as it's lost its youthful prettiness. And it seems a fair trade off."

The Oscar winner revealed whether or not she's gotten plastic surgery.

"My face is changing," she told Allure in an interview published August 2023, "and I love that my face is changing and aging. People think I had a facelift. They're like, 'What did she do to her face?' I'm like, 'Bitch, I'm just aging! It doesn't mean I got bad plastic surgery. This is just what happens.'"

The Pitch Perfect alum admitted she's never gotten any cosmetic injectables, telling People in 2023, "I've never put a needle in my face. And by the way, most people do it and truly, there's no judgement. But I make my living with my face."

She added, "Basically I'm terrified of f--king it up."

The Magic Mike actress set the record straight on whether or not she's gotten facial injectables. "No Botox!" she put it bluntly on Kelly Ripa's Let's Talk Off Camera podcast.

The "Summertime Sadness" singer denied having a surgical procedure on her nose after a fan referenced her "natural nose."

“Still never even been under the knife or anesthesia in my life for the 15th year in a row!!” Lana wrote on Instagram in September 2025, per a screenshot captured by People. “But if u use filler like [my doctor] used to- to build up the bridge of your nose it looks tall no bump. Takes seven minutes.”

The nonsurgical rhinoplasty Lana referred is “a cosmetic procedure where dermal fillers are used to temporarily change the shape of your nose,” according to the Cleveland Clinic. Though the procedure is less invasive, the results only last up to six months.

In 2021, the supermodel, who rose to fame in the '90s as one of the first, sued Zeltiq Aesthetics, alleging that its CoolScupting fat-reducing procedures that she underwent in 2015 and 2016 left her "permanently disfigured." The parties reached a settlement in the case in 2022.

In January 2021, while pregnant, the model wrote on her Instagram Story in response to fans' questions: "For anyone saying 'you need to stop w/ the lip injections': I've never had lip injections (no judging folks who do—ya'll look great!) but you can't even get injections when you're pregnant!"

Jenny from the Block continues to look like Jenny from the Block. In January 2021, she told an Instagram user, "I have never done Botox or any other injectables or surgery!! Just sayin'."

The Friends actress did have a nose job when she was younger to fix a deviated septum, but has spoke out against Botox and other facial fillers.

"There is also this pressure in Hollywood to be ageless," she told Yahoo! Beauty in 2014. "I think what I have been witness to, is seeing women trying to stay ageless with what they are doing to themselves. I am grateful to learn from their mistakes, because I am not injecting s--t into my face."

"I've probably tried everything. I would be scared to go under the knife, but you know, talk to me when I'm 50. I'll try anything. Except I won't do Botox again, because I looked crazy," the actress told Harper's Bazaar in 2013.

The Charlie's Angels alum told InStyle magazine in 2012, "I say, don't fight the rings on the trunk of a tree. Just keep counting 'em."

"The idea of not looking like myself scares me," she added.

The Love Actually actress told The Telegraph in 2011, "I'm not fiddling about with myself. We're in this awful youth-driven thing now where everybody needs to look 30 at 60."

"Nah. It's not my thing," the Oscar winner told MORE magazine in 2007. "I don't have anything against it for other people. Whatever they want to do, I'm fine with it. For me, it's really a self-image thing. Like, I'd rather have somebody go, "Wow, that girl has a big nose" than 'Wow, that girl has a bad nose job.' I'd rather have a comment about who I am than about something that identifies me as being ashamed of who I am."

In 2011, the pop star told Harper's Bazaar, "I think that promoting insecurity in the form of plastic surgery is infinitely more harmful than an artistic expression related to body modification."

In 2011, the Titanic star told the U.K. newspaper The Telegraph that cosmetic surgery goes against her morals, the way her parents brought her up and what she considers to be "natural beauty."

"I will never give in," she added. "I am an actress, I don't want to freeze the expression of my face."

#675. Steven Hack, Original ‘Cats’ Castmember and Busy Onscreen Character Actor, Dies at 68

His credits ranged from ‘Jake and the Fatman’ and ‘Seinfeld’ to ‘Pam & Tommy’ and ‘Amsterdam.’

Steven Hack, the theater veteran who spent five years on Broadway as an original castmember in Cats, then appeared as a character actor in dozens of films and TV shows, has died. He was 68.

Hack died Thursday at home following what was described as “a sudden and unexpected cardiac event,” the Interact Theatre Company announced. He was a founding member of the North Hollywood-based group that launched in 1989.

“Steven was a gifted and versatile performer, a superb graphic artist and a cherished member of our artistic family,” ITC directors Barry Heins and Walter Ware said in a statement. “His creativity and talent helped shape Interact in its earliest years, and his artistry, humor, warmth and generous spirit enriched everything he touched.” Related Stories Lifestyle The Pulitzer-Winning Play 'Purpose' Finally Came to Los Angeles. But That Doesn't Mean It's Gone Hollywood. Lifestyle 'The Comedy About Spies' to Open on Broadway This Spring

Born in St. Louis on April 20, 1958, Hack studied at CalArts and The American Academy of Dramatic Arts in Los Angeles. In 1978, he was a background dancer in the film version of Grease and appeared in the off-Broadway musical The Coolest Cat in Town.

Hack was there when Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Cats opened at the Winter Garden Theatre on Oct. 7, 1982, and he portrayed several characters, including Coricopat, Mungojerrie, Carbucketty, Tumblebrutus and Pouncival, over the next five years.

He toured with Michael Bennett’s A Chorus Line for nearly two years and then joined the Broadway production at the Shubert Theatre for one show only — its record-breaking 3,389th Great White Way performance on Sept. 29, 1983. (He did Cats that night, too.)

Hack started showing up on television in the 1990s on shows including The Trials of Rosie O’Neill, Jake and the Fatman, Matlock, Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman, Married … With Children, Seinfeld, Mad About You and Caroline in the City.

More recently, he found work in the series American Horror Story, Ratched, Perry Mason and Not Dead Yet, in the miniseries Pam & Tommy and Angelyne and in the films Thor: The Dark World (2013), Fantastic Four (2015), The Happytime Murders (2018) and Amsterdam (2022).

In 1995, he received an Ovation Award for his performance in an L.A. production of Elmer Rice’s venerable drama Counsellor-at-Law, then acted in the radio version for L.A. Theatre Works. And in 2003, he was nominated for another Ovation prize, this one for his turn in the Interact one-man drama Willie’s Son.
